title: Against Chamier: believing sins already remitted cannot be the justifying act
source_text: CIII. Chamierus tamen, & alii nonnulli volunt justificationem fidei tribuendam esse, ratione illius actus, quo credimus peccata nobis esse remissa. Sed haec sententia a vero prorsus aliena est. Quomodo enim possemus justificari per actum, qui justificationem jam factam praesupponit? Sed fiducia qua persuasum habemus peccata nobis jam esse condonata, supponit jam factam justificationem, siquidem jam justificatus est ille cui peccata remissa & condonata sunt. Concedit Chamierus, & qui cum eo sunt in ea sententia, hominem justificatum esse, & peccata esse remissa antequam credat. Sed hoc est toti Scripturae contrarium, quae perpetuo docet iram Dei super eum qui non credat manere, & fidem ac poenitentiam esse conditiones sub quibus nobis promittitur remissio peccatorum, & sine quibus illa haberi nequit. Adde quod qui justificatus est, hoc ipso est in statu gratiae, & Deo acceptus ad vitam aeternam. Sed impossibile est Deo placere sine fide; & qui nondum credit adhuc peccato servit, & filius est Diaboli & gehennae. Ut omittam quod jam dictum, omnino absurdum esse, si dicamus hominem justificari, per illud quod non praecedit justificationem, sed solum jam factam sequitur.
pass_a_gloss: Yet Chamier, and some others, want justification to be attributed to faith by reason of that act by which we believe that sins have been remitted to us. But this opinion is altogether alien from the truth. For how could we be justified by an act which presupposes justification already made? But the trust by which we have it persuaded that sins have already been forgiven to us presupposes justification already made, inasmuch as he to whom sins have been remitted and forgiven is already justified. Chamier, and those who are with him in that opinion, concede that a man is justified, and sins are remitted, before he believes. But this is contrary to the whole of Scripture, which perpetually teaches that the wrath of God remains upon him who does not believe, and that faith and repentance are the conditions under which remission of sins is promised to us, and without which it cannot be had. Add that he who is justified is by that very fact in the state of grace, and accepted by God unto eternal life. But it is impossible to please God without faith; and he who does not yet believe still serves sin, and is a son of the Devil and of gehenna. Not to mention what has already been said, that it is altogether absurd if we say a man is justified by that which does not precede justification, but only follows it already made.
pass_b_english: Chamier (and some): justify by the act of believing sins are already remitted — Le Blanc: wholly false.
That fiducia presupposes justification already done.
They concede a man is justified and sins remitted before he believes — against all Scripture: wrath remains on the unbeliever; faith and repentance are conditions of promised remission.
The justified are in grace and accepted for eternal life — yet without faith one cannot please God, and still serves sin.
Absurd to justify by what only follows justification.
